defects: Top-left and top-right captions sit directly on cracked, high-contrast ice. 'White is ice. The frame holds…' and 'September 2011: 4.56…' are partly cut through by crack lines and hard to read.
The 1979 caption has a flat grey plate behind it that is the only such plate in the film, so it looks pasted on.
Pairs 1/6 s apart are almost identical. In the ice shots, the melt front moves as a slow, linear crawl with no acceleration, settle or secondary motion.
The chart build (frame 4) shows bars appearing left to right at uniform spacing. The right half of the frame is empty, so this frame is just an unfinished state.
In the 3.57 shot, the stencil numerals are clipped by the ocean mask. The '.' and the lower half of the digits break up into ragged fragments instead of reading as a deliberate reveal.
On the end card, the Greenland shape is a flat red dashed blob with tiny source type set over busy ice. It doesn't match the finish of the rest of the film.
Each bar's crack texture is a crop of the same source, so the vertical joins repeat in a mechanical way at 100%.
gaps: Pacing and choreography: there are three shots of 12–13 s, each driven by one slow, constant-rate wipe of ocean into ice. Top studios would break each one into beats. The ice should crack, drift and settle with weight, and the camera should push and hold, so that each year lands as an impact instead of a dissolve.

Energy arc: the record low (2012 / 3.57) arrives around the midpoint, and the film then cuts to a chart that builds at an even rate. Nothing escalates toward a climax at 70–80%, and the Greenland payoff is underplayed instead of landing as the peak.

Sound: the spectrogram shows a static, harmonic drone bed with three clean broadband hits that do land on the cuts (~4.4 s, 13.1 s, 18.1 s) and one riser around 25 s. There is no ice-specific sound design (creaks, cracks, water) and little dynamic shape, so it reads as a generic pad rather than a scored, foley-rich mix.
